Clothes Distribution Initiative
New clothes for tribal families — restoring dignity where poverty had stolen modesty and hope

In the remote tribal areas of Gujarat, poverty is a way of life, indignity and mockery were accepted as natural as air and two full meals a day were a joyous occasion. Being fully clothed and protecting one's dignity was a distant dream for many of these tribals in the region. The women were the most adversely affected in this situation.
These were not just clothes — they were a promise that
would stand with them and protect their roots.

Taking advantage of this abject poverty and the resultant indignity, missionaries planted the seeds of hatred against Sanatan Dharma among these innocent and poor tribals. They whispered poisonous words — that the Vedic Gods had abandoned them, that Sanatan society had condemned them to eternal neglect. With sharp mockery, they pointed at the torn clothes of their children, sneering, "If your gods cared, would your little ones never know the softness of new fabric or the taste of good food?" Offering food, clothes and a show of love and respect, these vile missionaries lured many tribals away from their ancestral faith.

But as the saying goes, every dark cloud has a silver lining — Janswabhiman Welfare Society thundered its way through the darkness, promising unconditional love and respect. Through initiatives like the distribution of new clothes, they reached the hearts of the people. For the first time in years, tribal children giggled while wearing clean, colourful outfits, and women smiled through tears as they held garments that symbolized dignity restored.
For the first time in years, tribal children giggled while wearing clean, colourful outfits, and women smiled through tears as dignity was restored.

These were not just clothes — they were a promise! A promise that Jan Swabhiman would stand with them, protect their roots, and remind them that Sanatan Dharma never abandoned its own. As the world progressed and prospered, the rugged terrains of Dang, Tapi, Valsad, Narmada and adjoining areas struggled for basic needs. Women draped themselves in tattered sarees and children in worn rags often braved the world with little to shield their modesty. Where deception thrived, Jan Swabhiman stepped in with love and respect. The simple act of handing a neatly folded dress to a child or a fresh saree to a mother became a powerful restoration of dignity. Through love, service, and unbreakable commitment, Jan Swabhiman reminded these communities: "You are not forgotten. You are Sanatani. You are family. And you will always be protected!"

Compassion as Civilization: How Janswabhiman Restores the Sacred Bond with Gaumata
Reviving Sanatani values of Karuna, Jeevdaya, and Seva through dedicated Gauseva in Noida

The civilisation of Sanatan Dharma rose on the strength of values that honor life, karuna, Jeevdaya and Seva. Among the most enduring symbols of this ethos is Gaumata, revered not merely as a pashudhan (cattle wealth), but as a living embodiment of motherhood, nourishment and sattvic purity. But in the materialistic world of today, she becomes a victim of cruelty, exploitation and neglect — abandoned in its old age and living off its ‘utility’, injured or viciously attacked, or seized by ruthless slaughter mafia. Standing firmly against this apathy is Janswabhiman Welfare Society, whose Noida Gaushala revives the motherly bond between humans and Gaumata.
“धेनवः सर्वकामधुक्।” “Cows are the fulfillers of all rightful desires.” (

This Rigvedic Richa takes tangible form in our Gaushala — dedicated medical care, nutritious food, safe shelter, and emotional healing extended to more than three hundred rescued cows every month. As a living classroom, children visit the Gaushala, engage in Gauseva, learn about ecological harmony and participate in Havan and Pooja that nurture their samskaras. Families celebrate birthdays and special occasion performing havan, pooja and Gauseva, learning the Sanatani principles of Karuna and Seva.
Organic & Self-Reliant
“न हिंस्यान् सर्वभूतानि।” “Let no living being be harmed.” (Manusmriti 5.43)

This command, central to Dharmic ethics, guides every action of Janswabhiman Welfare Society. The Gaushala sustains itself through organic farming and eco-friendly practices. Here, Gaumata walks freely, calmed by trust, protected by dharmic values, and loved by our Gausevaks. In her serenity, society is reminded that when we protect the voiceless gentle, we recover the gentleness within ourselves.

A calf with severe dehydration may collapse, his tiny body unable to stand. Every delayed second in such a scenario pushes the jeev towards an untimely end.

But the Gausevaks of Janswabhiman Welfare Society put their all in trying to save the cherished Gauvansh and pull it out of its misery and suffering. Assam, 2024: When Floodwaters Rose, Dharma Walked In
Ration kits, medical aid and door-to-door relief when the Brahmaputra floods ravaged Assam

Every monsoon, the Brahmaputra unleashes its fury upon the innocent people of Assam, swallowing homes and lives. The fury-filled floods destroy everything in their paths, homes, livestock, food stocks and livelihood. The poor and the tribals living in the remote areas of the state are the worst affected, as they lose their all and are cut off from the main land, as village after villages disappear beneath muddy currents. In 2024, the floods returned with brutal force, ravaging settlements and destroying infrastructure. Villages were cut off for days. The promised relief aid never makes to these stranded villages and tribal settlements. Hunger, helplessness, diseases, apathy and neglect become the norm.
Every kit, every medicine, every clothes packet was handed with respect — “We are there for you, every step of the way!”

Janswabhiman Welfare Society stepped up in such excruciating circumstances for our brothers and sister in Assam. As waters raged, the team provided essentials, like dry ration kits, cooked food, clean drinking water, medicines and basic necessities to the affected people, door to door. Every kit, every medicine, every clothes packet was handed with respect, telling the flood-affected brethren “We are there for you, every step of the way!” Our team members never once hesitated to wade through deep waters- filled with filth and aquatic predators- to ensure every family and every animal was brought to safety. Distribution of adequate cooked food prevented starvation and hunger-fights. Medical aid helped prevent outbreak of diseases and infections.
Service rooted in Dharma never discriminates or abandons. It is like oxygen, available for all, while asking for nothing in return.

As floodwaters lingered, something else began to rise—resilience. In relief camps and partially submerged villages, Janswabhiman gave the courage, strength and every possible support to the people, to re-build their lives. For Assam’s flood-affected families, this relief work by Janswabhiman Welfare Society was not just an emergency aid- it was a morale booster and living proof that service rooted in Dharma never discriminates or abandons. It is like oxygen, available for all, while asking for nothing in return.

Walls rose, where there was only tattered cloth. For these displaced Hindus, every brick laid by Janswabhiman became a promise — that one who seeks refuge in Dharma’s lap shall never be abandoned.

His body shivers uncontrollably; dust mixes with blood as each breath drags pain deeper into his chest. Nearby, villagers gather helplessly, too afraid to touch him lest they worsen his injuries. The road where he grazed peacefully just hours ago has become a battlefield where he fights alone, losing strength with every passing minute.
Even in the ambulance,
treatment never stops
— painkillers, bandages and IV drips keep hope alive.

Responding to these kinds of emergencies, the trained Gausevaks of Jan Swabhiman Welfare Society rush in with medical kits, ropes and other necessary equipment and transport vehicles, if the need arises. Assessing injuries, they check the injured jeev for fractures, internal bleeding, and spinal damage. With teamwork, they slide a stretcher beneath his body, lifting him gently but firmly. Even in the ambulance, the treatment never stops — painkillers, bandages, IV drips are given to tide the injured bull through the pain. Even at the hospital or the Gaushala, with veterinarians around, the Gausevaks don't leave his side, whispering soothing words and stroking him gently to calm him down and reassure him.
His survival becomes a testament to human courage and compassion — one of the many goals of Janswabhiman.

Recovery may take days or even weeks. When he finally rises, the joy of the Gausevaks knows no bounds as they witness him trying to stand on his legs, however wobbly, and show to them that he has regained his strength. His survival becomes a testament to human courage and compassion — one of the many goals of Janswabhiman Welfare Society.

No visible wound — only fever, weakness and silent agony — until Gausevaks arrive with relief

When a revered Gaumata suffers, when no wound is visible, when no blood is seen oozing out, but the pain and helplessness due to illness and weakness weighs her down, only the heartless will not feel any sympathy and compassion. The once-strong mother now lies curled on the ground, her breath shallow, her body burning with fever. Her eyes, normally calm and nurturing, cloud over with confusion and pain. Whether from severe infections, digestive blockages, parasitic diseases, or untreated fevers, the silent agony consumes her. She cannot explain where it hurts, but only suffers silently, waiting for all of it to end, in a swoop of miracle.
Their seva proves that compassion and
— pillars of Sanatana Dharma — are the strongest medicine.

Janswabhiman Welfare Society is nothing short of a miracle for her and countless other jeevs like her. Upon receiving information of medical emergencies, the compassionate and well-trained Gausevaks rush to help their beloved Gaumata. Armed with medical kits, medicines, and deep knowledge earned from years of serving Gauvansh, the Gausevaks check her temperature and other vital functions, diagnose the issue and promptly work towards providing her relief. Saline drips are prepared in a few seconds flat; painkillers, antibiotics and other necessary medicines are administered with due precision. By this time, the other team members arrange for an ambulance.
When the fever breaks and she finally rises, they thank Ishwar — compassion proved stronger than illness.

They rush her with proper care to the veterinary hospital, whispering soothing words of reassurance in her ears, calming her nerves with gentle pet-strokes and massaging her limbs. Even in the hospital, they don't leave her side, ensuring every meal and every medicine are given on time, vitals are checked regularly. And when the fever breaks, when she finally rises after days of weakness, they heave a sigh of relief, thanking Ishwar for saving her precious life. Their seva is nothing but a proof that compassion and Jeevdaya, the pillars of Sanatana Dharma, are the strongest medicine.

Khambaliya Village, Vansda — July 2026 Floods
Rescue, cooked meals and medical aid when flash floods devastated Khambaliya village in Vansda, Gujarat

The skies unleashed their monsoon fury in and around Vansda taluka of Gujarat in July 2026, causing large scale devastating floods, displacing people, drowning livestock and snatching away livelihoods. The worst affected was the village of Khambaliya. The flash floods left the entire village craving for every grain of food, every shred of cloth and every drop of drinking water. The poor villagers were left waiting and praying for any help available.
Man and animal, all were rescued and tended to, alike, without any discrimination or conditions.

And help did come, in the form of Janswabhiman Welfare Society, who arrived armed with Dharmic values and compassion. The Janswabhiman Dharmasevaks rescued people stranded in their flooded homes and provided them with clothes, cooked meals thrice a day and medical aid. Our sevaks didn’t give a second thought to jump in the very strong currents of the floods, to rescue helpless people and livestock. Man and animal, all were rescued and tended to, alike, without any discrimination or conditions.
Dharma never abandons or discriminates — giving villagers the resilient strength to fight and win against any challenge.

Hunger-brawls and starvation were prevented through distribution of adequate cooked meals, epidemics and infections were fought against with the provision of medical aid. Women and girls, traumatised by the nature’s fury, were provided with hygiene products to ensure their physical well-being. As the flood waters receded, the hope and faith of the villagers was revived on the compassion and seva bhaav, the important pillars of Sanatan Dharma. It made them realise that Dharma never abandons or discriminates and gave them the resilient strength to fight and win against any challenge- natural or man-induced.

When Pain Turns Into a Cry for Help
Gausevaks racing through busy roads to rescue injured Gaumata — turning agony into hope
Gauseva & Animal Welfare

An injured Gaumata, lying helplessly and wailing in pain, on the streets, is a deplorable sight. With hope in her eyes, she gathers her strength to sit up but collapses back again, soaked in her own blood, flowing relentlessly and weakening her with every drop. People and vehicles pass her — either unaware or unwilling to stop. The gentle mother who once wandered freely now battles unbearable agony — deep cuts from sharp metal scraps, fractured limbs from speeding vehicles, or raw flesh torn from cruel attacks. Her eyes, dark and pleading, silently beg for relief that never seems to arrive. In these moments, she is not an animal — she is a suffering being, abandoned by the too-busy, inhumane world.
Not a single moment is wasted as
rush through busy roads — carrying medicines and hope for the injured jeev.

However, the Gausevaks of Janswabhiman Welfare Society are set apart from the rest of the world. Not a single moment is wasted as they rush through busy roads and narrow lanes, carrying medicines and hope for the injured jeev. With trained hands and disciplined coordination, they approach the wounded Gauvansh carefully, speaking softly to calm her trembling body. Ropes, stretchers, and makeshift supports are prepared within minutes. Every movement is deliberate — lifting her with care, stabilising bleeding wounds, and readying the vehicle for urgent transport to medical help.
When the Gaumata rises up, even if wobbly, it declares that humanity and compassion can restore hope to voiceless souls.

In the veterinary hospital or the Gaushala, under the supervision of the veterinarians, wounds are cleaned, fractures set, and drips administered. The Gausevaks stay throughout, fanning, feeding, and comforting the jeev until her breathing steadies. Some cases require days of watchful care, others months — yet the commitment never wavers. And when the Gaumata rises up, even if wobbly, it is more than just recovery — it is the moment which witnesses and declares that humanity and compassion — the basic principles of Sanatan Dharma — can bring about speediest recovery and hope in humanity in the hearts of these gentle voiceless souls.

content: Samuh Vivah (2019) · Jan Swabhiman Welfare Society · Janswabhiman
Vedic Samuh Vivahs that restored dignity, faith and cultural pride for tribal daughters of Tapi, Gujarat

Utter poverty, hunger and helplessness, societal apathy and neglect plagued the tribal region of Tapi in Gujarat. Two modest meals a day were luxury for most of the Hindu tribal people of the region. Schools, colleges and education were not even in the dreams of these families — struggling to make ends meet. Celebrating festivals was unheard of, with no lamps, feasts and festivities. Marriages were solemnised with the exchange of a packet of biscuits.
Marriages once solemnised with a packet of biscuits became Vedic Samuh Vivahs — sacred mantras, havan, and Kanya Maan restoring dignity to tribal daughters.

Adding to these woes were the sinister motives and tactics of cunning conversion agents. They ridiculed Sanatan traditions, twisting them into something vile. Kanyadaan, they mocked, was nothing but the "donation" of a daughter, proof — according to them — of Hinduism's disrespect for women. They jeered that Vedic Gods could not even provide food at weddings, that Sanatan Dharma was empty rituals, involving only fire which destroys everything, with no compassion. This evangelist venom found fertile ground in the disgruntled and frustrated hearts and minds of the tribal Hindus, who fell for the vile missionary conversion tactic dressed as concern.
In those moments, the tribals of Tapi did not just witness weddings; they witnessed the revival of faith, self-respect, and cultural pride.

This vicious attack on Sanatan Dharma was met with a thunderous reply by Janswabhiman Welfare Society. Organising Vedic Samuh Vivahs for tribal daughters across different villages, they brought back not only tradition but pride. The ceremonies echoed with sacred mantras, blazing havan fires, sindoor, mangalsutra, kanyadaan, and mangal pheras — every ritual infused with meaning, dignity, and grace. Afterward, grand feasts fed hundreds, proving that Sanatan Dharma does not abandon its children. Kanyadaan was revealed for its true essence — Kanya Maan, an act of honouring daughters as embodiments of Laxmi, entering their homes to be loved, respected, and cherished. In those moments, the tribals of Tapi did not just witness weddings; they witnessed the revival of faith, self-respect, and cultural pride.
